sections.title: Regulated Utility Operations
sections.subtitle: Customer connections and capital investment -- the two drivers of the regulated rate base

charts.title: Total Customer Connections
charts.annotation: FY2025: 3,242k water + 330k wastewater = 3,572k total. Water and wastewater are not split in the CSV; see the KPI cards above for the breakdown and the pending Essential Utilities merger (would add ~1.1m connections across 17 more states).

charts.title: CapEx & Operating Cash Flow
charts.annotation: CapEx here equals regulated capital investment ($3,200m in FY2025); management's 5-year plan is $19.0-20.0bn and its 10-year plan $46-48bn, funded by issuing equity and debt against the growing rate base, not out of free cash flow.

charts.title: Net Income vs Free Cash Flow vs Owner FCF
charts.annotation: Owner FCF, where shown, is the DCF's series after SBC, interest income and lease principal.

customers.title: Customer connections
customers.content:
Total customer connections is water plus wastewater service connections (one connection can serve a household, business or multi-unit building) -- the volume driver for a regulated utility's revenue, in thousands.

For American Water Works Company, Inc.: FY2025 connections were 3,242k water and 330k wastewater (3,572k total), serving roughly 14 million people across 24 states. Growth comes from organic adds (~19k/yr) plus bolt-on acquisitions (~21-70k/yr depending on deal flow), not population growth alone. The pending all-stock Essential Utilities merger would add roughly another 1.1 million connections across 17 additional states, making the combined company the clear industry leader (~4.7 million connections, ~$29.3bn combined rate base) -- but it has not closed: Pennsylvania reached a settlement in September 2026, other state approvals are still pending, and consumer advocates in Pennsylvania have formally opposed the deal.

What to watch:

  • Organic adds versus acquired connections (the latter costs cash up front, in exchange for a larger regulated rate base later)
  • Essential merger closing conditions and any divestitures required by regulators
  • Wastewater connections, still a small fraction of the total but the fastest-growing segment

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For American Water Works Company, Inc.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For American Water Works Company, Inc.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For American Water Works Company, Inc.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For American Water Works Company, Inc.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For American Water Works Company, Inc.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For American Water Works Company, Inc.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets -- for a regulated utility, mostly pipe replacement, treatment-plant upgrades and PFAS/lead compliance.

For American Water Works Company, Inc.: CapEx is regulated capital investment, run deliberately above operating cash flow ($3,200m vs. OCF in FY2025) and funded with new debt and equity, because every dollar invested grows the rate base on which the company earns its allowed ~9.5-10.95% return. Management's published plan is $19.0-20.0bn over 5 years and $46-48bn over 10, excluding any Essential Utilities merger impact.

What to watch:

  • CapEx tracking at or above the low end of the published 5-year plan
  • Equity issuance (including the unsettled forward-sale shares) funding the gap, which dilutes EPS before the new rate base earns a return
  • Allowed ROE trends across the 24 state jurisdictions

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For American Water Works Company, Inc.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For American Water Works Company, Inc.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For American Water Works Company, Inc.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
